This review included 406 independent writing treatment/control comparisons from pub- lished and unpublished studies involving 52,529 secondary students. All studies applied an experimental or quasi-experimental design (with pretests). When all writ- ing outcomes were considered collectively, teaching and practicing writing yielded a positive and statistically detectable effect size (ES) on students’ writing (0.47). When just specific writing outcomes were analyzed, writing instruction statisti- cally enhanced writing quality (ES = 0.46); ideation (ES = 0.46); text organization (ES = 0.51); inclusion of genre elements (ES = 0.60); voice (ES = 0.30); sentence construction skills (ES = 0.51); handwriting, spelling, and typing (ES = 0.49); plan- ning, revising, and writing self-regulation processes (ES = 0.82); knowledge about writing (ES = 0.94); and writing motivational beliefs (ES = 0.13). Graham and associates (2023) also examined if 23 specific writing interventions positively impacted secondary students’ writing outcomes. Statistically detectable positive effects were obtained for the following 17 writing practices: comprehensive writing programs (ES = 0.47); writing strategy instruction (ES = 0.76); use of digital writing tools (ES = 0.31); teaching handwriting, spelling, and/or typing (ES = 0.71); computer-assisted instruction (ES = 0.32); teaching critical/creative thinking skills for writing (ES = 0.27); emulating good models of writing (ES = 0.46); feedback (ES = 0.34); goal setting (ES = 0.44); pre-writing activities (ES = 0.49); gram- mar instruction (ES = 0.77); sentence instruction (ES = 0.73); inquiry (ES = 0.92); observing writers/readers (ES = 0.41); peer assistance (ES = 0.41); summarization instruction (ES = 0.49); and text structure instruction (ES = 0.39). es_descrip_explain: Overall, results showed a significant positive effect for mathematics outcomes (ES = +1.01), with a high variability suggesting the presence of factors influencing the effect. By analyzing these factors, the results showed a larger effect when the students involved had only math difficulties (ES = +1.04) compared to both math and reading difficulties (ES = +0.66). When the intervention was delivered in large groups (more than 8 students), the effect was larger than for one-to-one or small-groups (ES = +1.41, +0.86, respectively). Intensive interventions (3 to 5 times a week) were more effective than interventions implemented one or two times weekly (ES = +1.15, +0.76, respectively). A difference was also found for instructional model: interventions involving general heuristics were more effective than the ones based on schema-based instruction (ES = +1.18, +0.71, respectively). The overall effect was also influenced by methodological factors that should be considered. When only researchers delivered the intervention, the effect was higher compared to researchers plus school personnel as interventionists (ES = +1.23, +1.08, respectively). However, only interventions delivered by school personnel are easily replicable in regular school settings. Furthermore, when the effect was assessed with a measure developed by the researchers (ES = + 1.17) the effect was almost double than when measured by standardized tests (ES = + 0.59). The measure type is one of the most influential methodological factors in this meta-analysis together with group assignment and year of publication.

Among the participant variables, sample composition (group of children with mathematics difficulties vs. group of children with mathematics and reading difficulties) was the only characteristic that significantly influenced the effectiveness of problem-solving interventions. The effect of the interventions was stronger for children with mathematics difficulties than for children with mathematics and reading difficulties. The other variables studied, namely the child's school level and status (mathematics learning disability vs. children at risk of mathematics learning disability vs. mixed group including both types of children), did not influence the effectiveness of the interventions. However, the results corresponding to the child's status should be interpreted with caution due to the small sample of studies including children with difficulties in mathematics and reading. What are the intervention characteristics (e.g., group size) that influence the effectiveness of problem- solving interventions? Group size, frequency of intervention, and intervention approach influence the effectiveness of the intervention on problem solving. Large group interventions (greater than 8 participants) have a greater effect than small group interventions. This finding indicates that children with mathematics difficulties should first receive targeted instruction in large groups with their peers in general education classrooms (Powell et al., 2013). Children with mathematics difficulties then need support in smaller groups to specifically target the intervention (Fuchs et al., 2014). Furthermore, interventions delivered 3 to 5 times per week are more effective than interventions delivered 1 to 2 times per week. Intensive interventions that support children with mathematics difficulties are characterized by explicit instruction that promotes practice, ongoing progress monitoring, and feedback (Powell & Fuchs, 2015). Furthermore, more frequent mathematics interventions improve the quality of interactions with children as well as children's opportunities to optimize retention (Agarwal et al., 2015). Finally, the effect of interventions differs depending on the approach used. The authors distinguish two main groups of approaches: interventions based on modeling the semantic structure of the problem and heuristic interventions based on raising awareness of the problem-solving steps. According to the meta- analysis by Myers et al. (2022), the latter demonstrate a greater effect than the former, but both types of approach bring significant and positive effects
